Acceptance summary:

General value assessment: The brain is a hierarchically organized system. Is information in higher brain areas integrated over different time-scales than in lower brain areas? Gao et al. analyze intracranial recordings in humans across a large part of the neocortex using several new analytical techniques. They find that higher brain areas have longer neuronal time-scales. Neuronal time-scales are correlated with specific gene expression patterns, and are correlated with working memory performance.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Neuronal timescales are functionally dynamic and shaped by cortical microarchitecture" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by four peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Laura Colgin as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Thilo Womelsdorf (Reviewer #4).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, when editors judge that a submitted work as a whole belongs in eLife but that some conclusions require a modest amount of additional new data, as they do with your paper, we are asking that the manuscript be revised to either limit claims to those supported by data in hand, or to explicitly state that the relevant conclusions require additional supporting data.

Our expectation is that the authors will eventually carry out the additional experiments and report on how they affect the relevant conclusions either in a preprint on bioRxiv or medRxiv, or if appropriate, as a Research Advance in eLife, either of which would be linked to the original paper.

Summary:

Gao et al. analyze how brain-wide timescales of ECoG signals vary across the cortical hierarchy and relate these timescales to several other aspects of structure, behavior and function. They report the following main findings: 1) Timescales increase with the cortical hierarchy. 2) Time-scales, after regressing out the hierarchical T1w/T2w structure variable, correlate significantly with several genes related to synaptic receptors and ion channels. 3) Time-scales increase with working memory task vs. baseline, and predict working memory performance across subjects. 4) Time-scales decrease with aging, in a region-specific way. These findings are a significant advance in comparison to previous work by considering brain-wide hierarchy at a high spatial and temporal resolution and relating them to behaviour and genetics.

All four reviewers agreed the study is of substantial interest. The study was found of high quality.

Essential revisions:

1) Definition and comparison of timescales:

i) The comparison shown in Figure 2 between spiking time-scale and ECOG time-scale might be problematic, in the sense that the spiking time-scales were taken from the Murray et al., 2014 paper where they were quantified with a different technique. A possible solution would be to quantify time-scales in the same manner as Murray, or maybe there is a convincing argument why this is not a problem.

ii) For the non-specialist reader, the concept of neuronal timescales that is central to the paper should be defined more explicitly in the Introduction ('neuronal timescales' appear in paragraph three, while it gets defined in paragraphs one and two).

iii) Fast and slow responding to sensory versus cue related information may reflect a circular definition of timescales.

iv) The Results text says that the aperiodic components is interpreted as time scale but not how the inference is made, i.e. what quantity is interpreted as time scale.

v) It is difficult to keep track of which timescales are referred to when in the text, e.g. the authors start referring to neuronal timescales after having discussed ECOG based time scales and spike timescales. It seems important for cleanly separating the source of the timescale to denote them with a unique label depending on the source data that give rise to them. Why not using a subscript for spike, epiduralECoG, subduralECoG, intracranialLFP,.… ?

2) Timescales and hierarchy:

i) The correlations shown between transcriptomics and timescales need to be carefully considered. While the authors regress out T1w/T2w residuals, these might just be one structural factor that changes with cortical hierarchy and assumes that the underlying relationships are linear. Hence, it is possible that timescales and gene profiles are correlated with structure but that there is no causal relationship between these genes and timescales. In this sense, the correlation of genes with hierarchy might also yield similar genetic profiles. It would be important to show the correlation of hierarchy with genetic profiles, to see whether this looks different from the correlations that are obtained with timescale.

ii) The authors use T1W/T2W as the measure for cortical hierarchy. This is a gradient-based perspective on cortical hierarchy. However, there are other perspectives on hierarchy that are not gradient-based, but are based on anatomical connectivity, e.g. as pursued by Kennedy and Van Essen (Vezoli et al., 2020). This needs to be discussed.

iii) The manuscript addresses two distinct aspects of neuronal timescales: their relationship to local microarchitecture and their dynamics as a function of task or age. Although there is obviously a strong inter-relationship between these two aspects, this deserves a more extensive discussion. For example, in relation with the previous point, if local microstructural properties predict neuronal timescales, why is it that timescale changes during the delay seem to be ubiquitous (or are they)? And why should such changes (that are overall in the same range) correlate with subject performance in the PFC but not in the other areas? How does this relate to the aging observations? Although this discussion is bound to be speculative. It is important in order to strengthen the link between these two independent avenues of the paper, and to enrich the discussion about the functional role of these dynamic changes in neuronal timescales.

iv) The paper does not consider oscillations, which is fine, but the reader is left wondering how oscillations affect these time-scales. Discussion on this aspect would be useful.

4) Comments on figures, statistics and clarification:

i) Are the rho correlation values corrected for the expected value of the surrogate distribution? That is are they significantly overestimated due to the dependent samples issue? In this case it is recommended to report the corrected correlation values, rather than the raw correlation values.

ii) The correlation performed in Figure 4D is a bit unclear. Are the different dots+lines participants, or is this a binned correlation? If it is a binned correlation, does that represent a problem for the correlation analysis?

iii) It would be useful in Figure 1/2 to show some examples of ECOG time-scales related to the actual underlying signals and PSDs, rather than just illustrating the technique on simulated data, so that the validity of the technique can be judged.

iv) In general it would be useful to report carefully the N's and the dataset that is used for each analysis, because it is easy to get lost in what is what as the authors analyze a huge number of datasets.

v) The technique of removing spatial autocorrelations that influence the p-value appears to be sophisticated and well done. If the authors need another validation, one way of doing this would be to use a cross-validation prediction approach where a subset of subjects is used for training and the other subjects are used for testing.

vi) What are "these" limitations in the subsection “Neuronal timescale can be inferred from frequency domain”?

vii) Figure 1E: how is r2=1 when the dots do not fall on the line?

viii) The description of the methods needs be improved. For example, "we can estimate neuronal timescale from the 'characteristic frequency'" which implies a peak in the spectrum. Yet in the next sentence they write that they extract timescale from aperiodic components.

ix) Subsection “Synaptic and ion channel genes shape timescales of neuronal dynamics”: Are these markers also correlated with cell packing density? If so, it's possible that denser neural networks have longer timescales.

x) Relatedly, how strongly inter-correlated are these genetic markers across the cortex? The authors mostly take a mass-univariate approach except for showing gene-PC1 in Figure 3A. There isn't enough information shown to evaluate whether the top PC is suitable, or whether this PC comprises many/all gene contributions or is driven by a small number, etc.

xi) The modeling results seem to be missing. They appear as a schematic in Figure 1 and are mentioned in the Materials and methods section. Was this model actually used somewhere?

xii) In Figure 2B, some T1w/T2w values are above values of 2, which is not standard. Likewise, several outliers can be observed. This might have impacted the estimation of the regression slope. This slope currently matches the one from Burt et al., 2018, although the data point distribution is different.

xiii) Figure 4B is contradicting Figure 2C as the evidenced timescale hierarchy is different (comparing PC, PFC and OFC). Please explain.

xiv) Figure 4B and C, please show actual data points and justify parametric tests.

xv) Figure 4C: how consistent is the increase in delay period timescales across areas within each subject. In other words, is this a general property of the brain, task-related effects resulting in a non-specific adjustment in neuronal timescales or are there regional differences in the reported increase (you might want to exclude the PFC from the analysis to remove task related effects).

xvi) Given the described age-related effect, did the authors check that the different databases they used sampled from subjects with the same age distribution?

xvii) Legend of Figure 1 is not self-explanatory and a lot of the symbols and information plotted in the figures are not explained. Unfortunately, this information is also missing from the Results section.

5) General dense writing style and clarity:

The manuscript is written to be dense yet terse, which makes it harder to read, particularly given the complexity of the analyses. It feels like it was written for a journal with extreme word limitations. The manuscript would be overall improved if the authors would "loosen their belt" and explain the findings and methods in more detail. Figure legends should be more self-explanatory. Quite often, figure detail description and contextual information are missing both from the text and the figures. This also applies to the supplementary figures.

claims.source: While surface ECoG recordings offer much broader spatial coverage than extracellular single-unit recordings, they are fundamentally different signals: ECoG and field potentials largely reflect integrated synaptic and other transmembrane currents across many neuronal and glial cells, rather than putative action potentials from single neurons (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Figure 1A, yellow box).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ECoG signals supported by citation.

claims.claim: Neuronal spiking and transmembrane currents have distinct but related timescales of fluctuations.
claims.source: This suggests that neuronal spiking and transmembrane currents have distinct but related timescales of fluctuations, and that both are hierarchically organized along the primate cortex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between ECoG and single-unit timescales.

claims.claim: The neuronal timescale gradient overlaps with the dominant axis of gene expression across the human cortex (ρ = −0.60, p<0.001).
claims.source: Leveraging whole-cortex interpolation of the Allen Human Brain Atlas bulk mRNA expression (Gryglewski et al., 2018; Hawrylycz et al., 2012), we project voxel-wise expression maps onto the HCP-MMP1.0 surface parcellation, and find that the neuronal timescale gradient overlaps with the dominant axis of gene expression (i.e., first principal component of 2429 brain-related genes) across the human cortex (Figure 3A, ρ = −0.60, p<0.001; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for similar results with all 18,114 genes).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3A with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Timescales significantly correlate with the expression of NMDA receptor subunit gene GRIN2B.
claims.source: Consistent with theoretical predictions (Figure 3B), timescales significantly correlate with the expression of genes encoding for NMDA (GRIN2B) and GABA-A (GABRA3) receptor subunits, voltage-gated sodium (SCN1A) and potassium (KCNA3) ion channel subunits, as well as inhibitory cell-type markers (parvalbumin, PVALB), and genes previously identified to be associated with single-neuron membrane time constants (PRR5) (Bomkamp et al., 2019) (all Spearman correlations corrected for SA in gradients).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Timescales significantly correlate with the expression of GABA-A receptor subunit gene GABRA3.
claims.source: Consistent with theoretical predictions (Figure 3B), timescales significantly correlate with the expression of genes encoding for NMDA (GRIN2B) and GABA-A (GABRA3) receptor subunits, voltage-gated sodium (SCN1A) and potassium (KCNA3) ion channel subunits, as well as inhibitory cell-type markers (parvalbumin, PVALB), and genes previously identified to be associated with single-neuron membrane time constants (PRR5) (Bomkamp et al., 2019) (all Spearman correlations corrected for SA in gradients).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Timescales significantly correlate with the expression of voltage-gated sodium channel subunit gene SCN1A.
claims.source: Consistent with theoretical predictions (Figure 3B), timescales significantly correlate with the expression of genes encoding for NMDA (GRIN2B) and GABA-A (GABRA3) receptor subunits, voltage-gated sodium (SCN1A) and potassium (KCNA3) ion channel subunits, as well as inhibitory cell-type markers (parvalbumin, PVALB), and genes previously identified to be associated with single-neuron membrane time constants (PRR5) (Bomkamp et al., 2019) (all Spearman correlations corrected for SA in gradients).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Timescales significantly correlate with the expression of voltage-gated potassium channel subunit gene KCNA3.
claims.source: Consistent with theoretical predictions (Figure 3B), timescales significantly correlate with the expression of genes encoding for NMDA (GRIN2B) and GABA-A (GABRA3) receptor subunits, voltage-gated sodium (SCN1A) and potassium (KCNA3) ion channel subunits, as well as inhibitory cell-type markers (parvalbumin, PVALB), and genes previously identified to be associated with single-neuron membrane time constants (PRR5) (Bomkamp et al., 2019) (all Spearman correlations corrected for SA in gradients).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Timescales significantly correlate with the expression of inhibitory cell-type marker parvalbumin (PVALB).
claims.source: Consistent with theoretical predictions (Figure 3B), timescales significantly correlate with the expression of genes encoding for NMDA (GRIN2B) and GABA-A (GABRA3) receptor subunits, voltage-gated sodium (SCN1A) and potassium (KCNA3) ion channel subunits, as well as inhibitory cell-type markers (parvalbumin, PVALB), and genes previously identified to be associated with single-neuron membrane time constants (PRR5) (Bomkamp et al., 2019) (all Spearman correlations corrected for SA in gradients).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Timescales significantly correlate with the expression of gene PRR5 previously identified to be associated with single-neuron membrane time constants.
claims.source: Consistent with theoretical predictions (Figure 3B), timescales significantly correlate with the expression of genes encoding for NMDA (GRIN2B) and GABA-A (GABRA3) receptor subunits, voltage-gated sodium (SCN1A) and potassium (KCNA3) ion channel subunits, as well as inhibitory cell-type markers (parvalbumin, PVALB), and genes previously identified to be associated with single-neuron membrane time constants (PRR5) (Bomkamp et al., 2019) (all Spearman correlations corrected for SA in gradients).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance and is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Increased expression of NMDA receptor subunit 2B extends the NMDA current time course.
claims.source: More specifically, in vitro electrophysiological studies have shown that, for example, increased expression of receptor subunit 2B extends the NMDA current time course (Flint et al., 1997), while 2A expression shortens it (Monyer et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claims.claim: NMDA receptor subunit 2A expression shortens the NMDA current time course.
claims.source: More specifically, in vitro electrophysiological studies have shown that, for example, increased expression of receptor subunit 2B extends the NMDA current time course (Flint et al., 1997), while 2A expression shortens it (Monyer et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an in vitro study.

claims.claim: The GABA-A receptor time constant lengthens with increasing α3:α1 subunit ratio.
claims.source: Similarly, the GABA-A receptor time constant lengthens with increasing a3:a1 subunit ratio (Eyre et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Neuronal timescales positively correlate with GRIN2B and GABRA3 expression and negatively correlate with GRIN2A and GABRA1.
claims.source: We show that these relationships are recapitulated at the macroscale, where neuronal timescales positively correlate with GRIN2B and GABRA3 expression and negatively correlate with GRIN2A and GABRA1 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 3C and demonstrates macroscale recapitulation of in vitro findings.

claims.claim: Almost all genes related to voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channel alpha-subunits are correlated with timescale.
claims.source: Notably, almost all genes related to voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channel alpha-subunits—the main functional subunits—are correlated with timescale, while all inhibitory cell-type markers except parvalbumin have strong positive associations with timescale (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There is a significant correlation between single-cell and macroscale levels of association between gene expression and timescale (ρ = 0.36 and 0.25 for two datasets, p<0.001 for both).
claims.source: Comparing across these two scales for all previously identified timescale-related genes in two studies (N = 170 [Tripathy et al., 2017] and 4168 [Bomkamp et al., 2019] genes), we find a significant correlation between the strength of association at the single-cell and macroscale levels (Figure 3D, horizontal black lines; ρ = 0.36 and 0.25 for the two datasets, p<0.001 for both).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3D comparing single-cell and macroscale associations.

claims.claim: Genes highly associated with neuronal timescales are preferentially related to transmembrane ion transporter complexes, GABAergic synapses, and chloride channels.
claims.source: We find that genes highly associated with neuronal timescales are preferentially related to transmembrane ion transporter complexes, as well as GABAergic synapses and chloride channels (see Figure 3F and Supplementary file 1 for GOEA results with brain genes only, and Supplementary file 2 for all genes).
claims.evidence: This finding is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Genes negatively associated with timescale are related to transmembrane transporters and voltage-gated ion channels, especially potassium and other inorganic cation transporters.
claims.source: Conversely, genes that are negatively associated with timescale are related to numerous groups involved in the construction and functioning of transmembrane transporters and voltage-gated ion channels, especially potassium and other inorganic cation transporters.
claims.evidence: This finding is from the gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Baseline neuronal timescales follow a hierarchical progression across association regions (parietal cortex, PFC, OFC, and MTL).
claims.source: Replicating our previous result in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G, we observe that baseline neuronal timescales follow a hierarchical progression across association regions, where parietal cortex (PC), PFC, OFC, and MTL have gradually longer timescales (pairwise Mann–Whitney U-test, Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4B based on working memory task data.

claims.claim: Timescales in all regions are approximately 20% longer during delay periods compared to baseline.
claims.source: Consistent with our prediction, timescales in all regions are ~20% longer during delay periods (Figure 4C; Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
claims.evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4C with statistical testing.

claims.claim: Only timescale changes in the PFC are significantly correlated with working memory performance across participants (ρ = 0.75, p=0.003).
claims.source: Moreover, only timescale changes in the PFC are significantly correlated with behavior across participants, where longer delay-period timescales relative to baseline are associated with better working memory performance (Figure 4D, ρ = 0.75, p=0.003).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: No other spectral features show consistent changes from baseline to delay periods while also significantly correlating with individual performance.
claims.source: No other spectral features in the recorded brain regions show consistent changes from baseline to delay periods while also significantly correlating with individual performance, including the 1/f-like spectral exponent, narrowband theta (3–8 Hz), and high-frequency (high gamma; 70–100 Hz) activity power (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Older adults have faster neuronal timescales (ρ = −0.31, p=0.010).
claims.source: We observe that older adults have faster neuronal timescales (ρ = −0.31, p=0.010; Figure 4E), and that timescales shorten with age in most areas across the cortex (Figure 4F, t = −7.04, p<0.001; 114 out of 189 parcels where at least six participants have data, see Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 4E based on analysis of the MNI-iEEG dataset.

claims.claim: Timescales shorten with age in most areas across the cortex (t = −7.04, p<0.001).
claims.source: We observe that older adults have faster neuronal timescales (ρ = −0.31, p=0.010; Figure 4E), and that timescales shorten with age in most areas across the cortex (Figure 4F, t = −7.04, p<0.001; 114 out of 189 parcels where at least six participants have data, see Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4F with statistical testing.

claims.claim: Timescale compression with aging is especially prominent in sensorimotor, temporal, and medial frontal regions.
claims.source: This timescale compression is especially prominent in sensorimotor, temporal, and medial frontal regions.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the aging analysis.

claims.claim: Neuronal timescales estimated from transmembrane current fluctuations can rapidly shift in a functionally relevant manner.
claims.source: These results support our hypothesis that neuronal timescales, estimated from transmembrane current fluctuations, can rapidly shift in a functionally relevant manner, as well as slowly—over decades—in healthy aging.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the working memory and aging results.

claims.claim: There exist multiple different quantities that can be considered as characteristic neuronal timescales across several spatial scales.
claims.source: Similarly, it is important to note that there exist many different quantities that can be considered as characteristic neuronal timescales across several spatial scales, including membrane potential and synaptic current timescales (Duarte et al., 2017), single-unit spike-train timescales (Murray et al., 2014), population code timescales (Runyan et al., 2017), and even large-scale circuit timescales measured from the fMRI BOLD signal (Watanabe et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual point supported by citations to different types of timescale measurements.

claims.claim: Timescales inferred from ECoG are consistently approximately 10 times faster than single-unit spiking timescales in macaques.
claims.source: We show here that timescales inferred from ECoG are consistently approximately 10 times faster than single-unit spiking timescales in macaques, corroborating the fact that field potential signals mainly reflect fast transmembrane and synaptic currents (Buzsáki et al., 2012), whose timescales are related to, but distinct from, single-unit timescales measured in previous studies (Dotson et al., 2018; Ogawa and Komatsu, 2010; Wasmuht et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the macaque comparison results with supporting citations.

claims.claim: A similar gradient of oscillatory timescales exists along the anterior–posterior axis of the human cortex.
claims.source: Furthermore, while we specifically investigate here the aperiodic timescale, which corresponds to the exponential decay timescale measured in previous studies, recent work has shown a similar gradient of oscillatory timescales (i.e., frequency) along the anterior–posterior axis of the human cortex (Mahjoory et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent work.

claims.claim: Gene expression levels are highly correlated with the percentage of cells expressing that gene within brain regions.
claims.source: In general, gene expression levels are highly correlated with the percentage of cells expressing that gene within brain regions (Lein et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claims.claim: Neurotransmitter receptor density measured via autoradiography follows similar cortical gradients.
claims.source: Furthermore, recent works have shown that neurotransmitter receptor density measured via autoradiography in postmortem brains follows similar cortical gradients (Goulas et al., 2020), and that gene expression levels of neurotransmitter receptors (e.g., 5HT) are strongly correlated with ligand binding potential measured via PET (Gryglewski et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work.

claims.claim: Transmembrane current timescales across multiple association regions increase during the delay period of a working memory task.
claims.source: Transmembrane current timescales across multiple association regions, including parietal, frontal, and medial temporal cortices, increase during the delay period of a working memory task, consistent with the emergence of persistent spiking during working memory delay.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the working memory findings.

claims.claim: Working memory performance across individuals is predicted by the extent of timescale increase in the PFC only.
claims.source: Working memory performance across individuals, however, is predicted by the extent of timescale increase in the PFC only.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the working memory analysis.

claims.claim: Neuronal timescale shortens with age in most cortical regions.
claims.source: In the long term, we find that neuronal timescale shortens with age in most cortical regions, linking age-related synaptic, cellular, and connectivity changes—particularly those that influence neuronal integration timescale—to the compensatory posterior-to-anterior shift of functional specialization in healthy aging (Davis et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the aging findings with supporting citation.

claims.claim: Structural properties may constrain dynamical properties to a possible range within a particular brain region.
claims.source: We speculate that structural properties may constrain dynamical properties (such as timescale) to a possible range within a particular brain region and at different spatial scales, while task requirements, input statistics, short-term synaptic plasticity, and neuromodulation can then shift timescale within this range.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: Only shifts in dynamics within the area of relevance are indicative of task performance.
claims.source: We posit, then, that only shifts in dynamics within the area of relevance (i.e., PFC for working memory) are indicative of task performance, consistent with recent ideas of computation-through-dynamics (Vyas et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the working memory findings and citation.

claims.claim: Consistent and converging patterns exist between transcriptomics, anatomy, dynamics, and function across multiple datasets.
claims.source: In summary, we identify consistent and converging patterns between transcriptomics, anatomy, dynamics, and function across multiple datasets of different modalities from different individuals and multiple species.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: The introduction of an open-source toolbox allows for noninvasive estimation of neuronal timescales using EEG and MEG.
claims.source: Furthermore, the introduction and validation of an open-source toolbox (Donoghue et al., 2020) for inferring timescales from macroscale electrophysiological recordings potentially allows for the noninvasive estimation of neuronal timescales, using widely accessible tools such as EEG and MEG.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the toolbox and represents a methodological contribution.

claims.claim: Neuronal timescale is defined as the exponential decay time constant (τ) of the empirical autocorrelation function.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies, we define 'neuronal timescale' as the exponential decay time constant (τ) of the empirical ACF, or lagged correlation (Honey et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citations.

claims.claim: PSDs are estimated using a modified Welch's method where the median is taken across time instead of the mean.
claims.source: PSDs are estimated using a modified Welch's method, where short-time windowed Fourier transforms (STFT) are computed from the time series, but the median is taken across time instead of the mean (in conventional Welch's method) to minimize the effect of high-amplitude transients and artifacts (Izhikevich et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological approach with citation.

claims.claim: The MNI-iEEG dataset has coverage in 178 of 180 parcels with at least one patient having an electrode within 4 mm.
claims.source: While coverage is sparse and idiosyncratic in individual patients, it does not vary as a function of age, and when pooling across the entire population, 178 of 180 parcels have at least one patient with an electrode within 4 mm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
claims.evidence: This describes the electrode coverage in the dataset, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: T1w/T2w ratio captures gray matter myelination and indexes the proportion of feedforward vs. feedback connections between cortical regions.
claims.source: We then compare the timescale gradient to the average T1w/T2w map from the Human Connectome Project, which captures gray matter myelination and indexes the proportion of feedforward vs. feedback connections between cortical regions, thus acting as a noninvasive proxy of connectivity-based anatomical hierarchy (Burt et al., 2018; Glasser and Van Essen, 2011).
claims.evidence: This describes the T1w/T2w measure with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Moran Spectral Randomization performs eigendecomposition on a spatial weight matrix to generate randomized null feature maps that preserve autocorrelation.
claims.source: Briefly, MSR performs eigendecomposition on a spatial weight matrix of choice, which is taken here to be the inverse average geodesic distance matrix between all pairs of parcels in HCP-MMP1.0. The eigenvectors of the weight matrix are then used to generate randomized null feature maps that preserves the autocorrelation of the empirical map.
claims.evidence: This describes the MSR method for generating spatial autocorrelation-preserving null maps.

claims.claim: PCA factorizes the gene expression matrix X such that X = USVT.
claims.source: PCA was computed on the variance-normalized average gene expression maps, X, an N × P matrix where N = 18,114 (or N = 2429 brain-specific) genes, and P = 180 cortical parcels. Briefly, PCA factorizes X such that X = USVT, where U and V are unitary matrices of dimensionality N × N and P × P, respectively.
claims.evidence: This describes the mathematical basis of PCA.

claims.claim: Fourteen unique participants were analyzed from the working memory ECoG datasets.
claims.source: Subject 3 (s3) from fcx-2 was discarded due to poor data quality upon examination of trial-averaged PSDs (high noise floor near 20 Hz), while s5 and s7 from fcx-3 correspond to s5 and s8 in fcx-2 and were thus combined. Together, data from 14 unique participants (22–50 years old, five females) were analyzed, with variable and overlapping coverage in PC (n = 14), PFC (n = 13), OFC (n = 8), and MTL (n = 9).
claims.evidence: This describes the participant sample for the working memory analysis.

claims.claim: 900 ms of data from pre-trial baseline and delay periods were analyzed for the working memory task.
claims.source: For our analysis, we collapsed across the stimulus context conditions and compared neuronal timescales during the last 900 ms of baseline and delay periods from the epoched data, which were free of visual stimuli, in order to avoid stimulus-related event-related potential effects.
claims.evidence: This describes the data selection for the working memory analysis.

results.result: Neuronal timescales inferred from human intracranial ECoG recordings increase along the sensorimotor-to-association axis across the entire human cortex and are negatively correlated with T1w/T2w ratio (ρ = −0.47, p<0.001), indicating alignment with anatomical hierarchy.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C28-C31, and C75 collectively demonstrate that the frequency-domain method for estimating timescales was validated on simulated data (C28), applied to a large human ECoG dataset with broad cortical coverage (C29, C75), and revealed a gradient of timescales that increases from sensory to association regions (C5, C30) and correlates significantly with anatomical hierarchy measured by T1w/T2w (C31). The statistical significance was corrected for spatial autocorrelation, and the findings are supported by convergent evidence from multiple analyses.

results.result: Human cortical timescales scale with single-unit timescales within macaques, with ECoG-derived timescales being consistently approximately 10 times faster than single-unit spiking timescales, suggesting that neuronal spiking and transmembrane currents have distinct but related timescales of fluctuations.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C33, C36, and C61 demonstrate cross-species and cross-scale validation. The comparison between human ECoG timescales and macaque single-unit timescales (from independent datasets) shows strong correlation (ρ = 0.96, p<0.001) with a consistent ~10x scaling factor. This is consistent with the known biophysical basis that ECoG reflects transmembrane currents rather than action potentials (C33), supporting the inference that these represent related but distinct timescales (C36, C61).

results.result: Cortex-wide transcriptomic analysis shows that neuronal timescales align with the dominant axis of gene expression (ρ = −0.60, p<0.001) and significantly correlate with expression of excitation- and inhibition-related genes (GRIN2B, GABRA3, GRIN2A, GABRA1), voltage-gated ion channel genes (SCN1A, KCNA3), and inhibitory cell-type markers (PVALB), with correlations corrected for spatial autocorrelation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C37-C43, C47, and C48 provide converging evidence from transcriptomic analysis. The timescale gradient overlaps with PC1 of gene expression (C37), and specific genes known from in vitro studies to affect synaptic and membrane timescales show significant correlations at the macroscale (C38-C43, C47). The finding that almost all voltage-gated sodium and potassium channel alpha-subunits correlate with timescale (C48) strengthens the biological plausibility. All correlations were corrected for spatial autocorrelation, addressing a key statistical concern.

results.result: There is a significant correlation between single-cell and macroscale levels of association between gene expression and timescale (ρ = 0.36 and 0.25 for two datasets, p<0.001 for both), demonstrating that single-cell electrophysiology-transcriptomic relationships are recapitulated at the macroscale.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 demonstrates cross-scale validation by comparing associations between gene expression and timescale at single-cell (from patch-clamp and scRNAseq data) and macroscale (from ECoG and bulk mRNA) levels. The significant correlations (ρ = 0.36 and 0.25, p<0.001) across two independent single-cell datasets provide strong evidence that microscale mechanisms scale to macroscale dynamics. This is a critical validation that strengthens causal interpretations.

results.result: Gene ontology enrichment analysis reveals that genes highly associated with neuronal timescales (after regressing out T1w/T2w) are preferentially related to transmembrane ion transporter complexes, GABAergic synapses, and chloride channels, while genes negatively associated are related to voltage-gated potassium and other inorganic cation transporters.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C51 describe results from gene ontology enrichment analysis (GOEA) that identified specific functional gene clusters associated with timescales beyond what is explained by anatomical hierarchy (T1w/T2w was regressed out). The enrichment of ion transporter and GABAergic synapse genes is biologically plausible and consistent with theoretical predictions. The control analysis using T1w/T2w instead of timescales yielded less specific results, supporting the specificity of these findings to timescale dynamics.

results.result: Prefrontal cortex timescales expand by approximately 20% during working memory maintenance delay periods compared to baseline, and the extent of PFC timescale expansion significantly predicts individual working memory performance across participants (ρ = 0.75, p=0.003), while timescales in other association regions (parietal, orbitofrontal, medial temporal) also increase but do not predict performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C52-C54, C65, and C66 collectively demonstrate functional dynamics of timescales during working memory. The ~20% increase in timescales during delay periods across multiple association regions (C53) is statistically significant (Wilcoxon rank-sum test), and the specific correlation between PFC timescale changes and behavioral performance (C54, ρ = 0.75, p=0.003) provides strong evidence for functional relevance. The regional specificity (only PFC predicts performance, C54, C66) strengthens the interpretation that timescale dynamics are functionally meaningful rather than epiphenomenal.

results.result: Cortex-wide timescales compress (shorten) with aging, with older adults showing faster neuronal timescales (ρ = −0.31, p=0.010), and timescales shortening with age in most cortical regions (t = −7.04, p<0.001; 114 of 189 parcels), especially in sensorimotor, temporal, and medial frontal regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C56-C58, and C67 demonstrate long-term changes in timescales with aging. The negative correlation between age and timescales (C56, ρ = −0.31, p=0.010) is statistically significant, and the widespread nature of this effect across most cortical parcels (C57, t = −7.04, p<0.001) is robust. The regional specificity (C58) adds biological plausibility. The analysis appropriately controlled for spatial sampling bias by normalizing parcels before averaging within participants, addressing a key methodological concern.

results.result: No other spectral features (1/f-like spectral exponent, narrowband theta power, high-frequency gamma power) show consistent changes from baseline to delay periods while also significantly correlating with individual working memory performance.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 provides important negative control evidence that strengthens the specificity of the timescale-behavior relationship (C54). By demonstrating that other commonly studied spectral features do not show the same pattern of task-related changes and behavioral correlations, this supports the interpretation that timescale is a functionally distinct and relevant measure. The evidence is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

results.result: Timescales are positively correlated with cortical thickness (ρ = 0.37, p=0.035), another index of cortical hierarchy that is itself anti-correlated with T1w/T2w.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 provides additional structural validation by showing correlation with cortical thickness, another measure of cortical hierarchy. The correlation is statistically significant (p=0.035) and consistent with the T1w/T2w findings. However, this is a supporting finding rather than a primary result, as cortical thickness is noted to be anti-correlated with T1w/T2w, making it somewhat redundant with the T1w/T2w analysis.

results.result: The frequency domain approach for estimating timescale is advantageous when a variable power law exponent and strong oscillatory components are present, and extracted timescales from simulated neural time series closely match their ground-truth values.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C28 describe and validate the methodological approach. The validation on simulated data (C28, Figure 1E) demonstrates that the method accurately recovers ground-truth timescales. The advantage over time-domain methods (C27) is supported by citation and reasoning about the presence of oscillatory components and variable power law exponents in neural data. This is a methodological validation rather than a primary scientific finding.

results.result: Neuronal timescales follow cytoarchitectonic gradients across the human cortex and are functionally dynamic, relevant for cognition in both short and long terms, bridging microcircuit physiology with macroscale dynamics and behavior, with consistent and converging patterns between transcriptomics, anatomy, dynamics, and function across multiple datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C59, and C70 represent high-level summary conclusions that integrate findings from multiple analyses. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective evidence from structural correlations (C31, C32), transcriptomic associations (C37-C51), functional dynamics during working memory (C52-C54), and aging effects (C56-C58). The claim of 'bridging' scales is justified by the cross-scale validation (C49, C61) and convergence across multiple independent datasets and modalities.

results.result: Structural properties may constrain dynamical properties (such as timescale) to a possible range within a particular brain region, while task requirements and neuromodulation can shift timescale within this range, and only shifts in dynamics within the area of relevance (i.e., PFC for working memory) are indicative of task performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C69 represent speculative interpretations and hypotheses rather than direct findings. While these interpretations are consistent with the data (stable structural gradients coexisting with dynamic functional changes, and regional specificity of behavior-timescale correlations), they go beyond what is directly demonstrated. The proposed mechanisms (neuromodulation, task requirements) are not tested in this study. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but should not be considered established results.

results.result: The introduction and validation of an open-source toolbox allows for noninvasive estimation of neuronal timescales using widely accessible tools such as EEG and MEG.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 suggests that the toolbox enables noninvasive estimation of timescales using EEG and MEG, but this study only validates the method on invasive ECoG recordings and simulated data. While the toolbox (Donoghue et al., 2020) may be applicable to EEG/MEG, this claim is not directly supported by data presented in this manuscript. The potential for noninvasive application is speculative and would require separate validation.

results.result: Background claims establishing the theoretical and empirical context for the study, including that cognitive functions require information maintenance over multiple timescales, theoretical accounts predict hierarchical timescales, and prior evidence from animal studies and human neuroimaging suggests such hierarchies exist but direct electrophysiological evidence across the human cortex is lacking.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C13-C20 represent background knowledge and literature review that establishes the motivation and context for the study. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to prior work and represent accurate characterizations of the existing literature. Claim C3 correctly identifies the gap that this study addresses. These are not results of the current study but rather establish the scientific context.

results.result: Methodological and dataset description claims, including definitions of neuronal timescale, descriptions of the datasets used (MNI-iEEG, HCP, working memory ECoG), and details of analytical procedures (PSD estimation, spatial autocorrelation correction, PCA).
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C29, C60, C72, C73, C75-C80 describe methodological details, dataset characteristics, and analytical procedures.
